content: The recovery rates for children with nutritional oedema treated in outpatient care were reported in several studies. In one subgroup of 171 children treated exclusively in outpatient settings, the recovery rate was 89%. Another study in Bangladesh compared recovery rates among children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) who were treated in inpatient care, day care, and home care after one week of day care. The recovery rates were 87%, 67%, and 75%, respectively. At the start of home care, 80% of children still had oedema, but all eventually recovered. Notably, no food supplements were provided to the home care group. Mortality rates for children with nutritional oedema treated in outpatient care ranged from 1% to 4% across six studies, but one study in Malawi reported a peak mortality rate of 16% among children with kwashiorkor. In this study, 70% of deaths occurred during inpatient care, with 53% occurring within the first four days of admission, suggesting the presence of medical complications, potentially linked to high HIV prevalence. Mortality rates were lower in children with kwashiorkor (16%) compared to those with marasmus (47%) or marasmic kwashiorkor (42%). Across four studies, mortality rates for children treated in outpatient care were consistently lower for kwashiorkor (0%-4%) than for marasmus (4%-5%) or marasmic kwashiorkor (7%-14%). The median time to recovery in outpatient care was reported in two studies, ranging from 35 to 42 days. In one study, the median recovery time was similar for kwashiorkor and marasmus cases but longer for marasmic kwashiorkor cases. However, weight gain after oedema resolution was slower in the kwashiorkor group. A study in Bangladesh found that children treated at home took longer to lose oedema (19 days) and recover (35 days) compared to those in day care (13 and 23 days) or inpatient care (11 and 18 days). Weight gain after oedema resolution was also slower in the home care group, which received no nutritional support. The quality of evidence across studies was low. Definitions of oedema were poorly described, and anthropometric measurements lacked precision and accuracy. Weight gain was often measured during the first four weeks of treatment, but it was unclear whether this was assessed after oedema resolution. Only three studies reported on mean length/height and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) gains in children with oedema treated in outpatient care. The rate of MUAC and length gain was higher in outpatient care compared to inpatient care in one study. Cost-effectiveness was explored in one study, which found that home-based treatment was four times more cost-effective than inpatient care. However, parental costs were highest for home care due to the lack of food supplementation. Another review highlighted the scarcity of experimental evidence on the cost-effectiveness of community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) and called for more rigorous evaluations. Infection rates were examined in one study, which found that children managed in inpatient settings had twice the incidence of infection symptoms (fever, cough, diarrhea) compared to those in home-based treatment with ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF). This may have contributed to the higher mortality and lower recovery rates in the inpatient group. Overall, outpatient treatment of nutritional oedema appears to be effective, with recovery rates exceeding 87% and case fatality rates below 4%. Default rates were below 10%, indicating acceptability among caregivers. However, the quality of evidence was low, and further high-quality studies are needed to provide conclusive guidance. Outcomes stratified by oedema severity (+/++/+++) are particularly needed. Additionally, marasmic kwashiorkor patients had higher risks of death and complications, requiring intensive care and cautious feeding regimens that are not feasible in outpatient settings. International guidelines recommend antibiotics as part of SAM case management in outpatient care, but only four of eight studies included in this review systematically prescribed antibiotics. This did not appear to impact mortality or recovery rates. Future randomized controlled trials should assess cost-effectiveness, coverage, and stratified outcomes to improve the management of nutritional oedema in outpatient settings.
